text: Maize streak virus (MSV) causes pale to yellow streaks that run parallel to the leaf veins, often starting as small scattered spots that merge into broken lines along the length of the leaf. Infected plants are stunted, with shortened internodes and poor cob formation when infected early. The virus is spread by leafhoppers (Cicadulina species), not by seed or soil, so spread follows leafhopper movement from nearby grasses and volunteer maize. Management is preventive: plant early and uniformly in the season to escape peak leafhopper flights, remove volunteer maize and grassy hosts, and use tolerant varieties where available. There is no curative spray for the virus itself.

Nitrogen deficiency in maize shows first on the oldest, lowest leaves because nitrogen is mobile and the plant moves it to new growth. The classic sign is a yellowing that begins at the leaf tip and runs down the midrib in a V-shape, with the lower leaves going pale or firing while the youngest top leaves stay greener. Growth is slow and plants are spindly. It is common on sandy soils and after heavy rain leaches nitrogen below the root zone. Correct by top-dressing a nitrogen source at the rate on the product label or as advised by a local extension officer, split to match crop demand, and avoid waterlogging that drives further leaching.

Sulphur deficiency in maize resembles nitrogen deficiency but appears first on the YOUNGEST top leaves rather than the old lower ones, because sulphur is not readily remobilised within the plant. The whole young leaf pales to a uniform light green or yellow without the V-shaped tip pattern of nitrogen. It occurs on sandy, low-organic-matter soils and where only nitrogen-phosphorus fertilisers have been used for years. Which leaves are worst — old or young — is the quickest way to tell sulphur and nitrogen apart in the field.

Fall armyworm caterpillars feed inside the maize whorl, leaving ragged holes, torn leaves, and moist sawdust-like frass (droppings) in the funnel. Damage is worst on young vegetative plants and can move to the developing cob. Scout weekly from emergence, looking into the whorl. Early hand-picking of egg masses and young larvae, encouraging natural enemies, and keeping plants well nourished all help. For any insecticide, follow the product label rate and local extension guidance; never guess a dose.

Newcastle disease is a highly contagious viral disease of poultry that can cause sudden death with high mortality across a flock. Signs include coughing, gasping and other respiratory distress, nasal discharge and watery or swollen eyes, greenish diarrhoea, and nervous signs such as twisted necks or paralysis in survivors. Because several birds can die quickly and the whole flock is at risk, rapid response matters: isolate affected birds, avoid moving birds or eggs off the property, and dispose of dead birds safely. There is no treatment for the virus; control is by routine vaccination and biosecurity. Report suspected outbreaks to a veterinary officer.

Newcastle disease is prevented, not cured. In smallholder flocks, thermotolerant vaccines such as the I-2 strain can be given by eye-drop and are widely used where cold chain is limited. A typical village programme vaccinates every few months and repeats after adding new birds, but exact schedule, dose and handling must follow the vaccine label and the advice of a local veterinary or extension officer. Alongside vaccination, keep new or sick birds separate, limit visitors to the flock, and clean drinkers and feeders regularly.

Infectious bronchitis is a viral respiratory disease of chickens causing coughing, sneezing, gasping, and nasal and eye discharge, usually with lower mortality than Newcastle disease unless complicated by other infections. In layers it causes a drop in egg production and misshapen, soft-shelled eggs. It spreads rapidly by air and contact. Supportive care — warmth, good ventilation without draughts, and clean water — helps recovery, and vaccination programmes exist. Because respiratory signs overlap with Newcastle disease and fowl cholera, sudden high death losses should be treated as possible Newcastle and reported to a vet.

Fowl cholera is a bacterial disease (Pasteurella multocida) that can cause sudden death in poultry, sometimes with swollen wattles, lameness, greenish diarrhoea, and nasal discharge. Unlike the purely viral respiratory diseases it can respond to antibiotics, but the choice, dose and withdrawal period must be set by a veterinarian — do not self-prescribe. Prevention rests on clean water, rodent control, removing carcasses promptly, and not mixing sick birds with healthy ones.

Young chicks cannot regulate their own temperature and their behaviour under the brooder lamp is the best thermometer. Chicks spread evenly, moving, feeding and chirping softly are comfortable. Chicks huddled tightly right under the lamp and cheeping loudly are too cold. Chicks pushed to the edges, panting with wings held away from the body, are too hot. Chicks piled into one corner usually signals a draught. Piling and smothering — where birds crowd together at night from cold, a draught, or a fright and the ones underneath suffocate — is a common cause of steady night losses in otherwise healthy-looking birds; you find them heaped together rather than scattered.

Steady losses at night in fast-growing broilers, with birds that looked healthy by day, point more often to management and environment than to a fast-spreading disease. Common causes are piling or smothering (birds found heaped in a corner from cold, draught or a night fright), sudden death syndrome or 'flip-over' in well-fleshed broilers (found on their backs, scattered rather than piled), and night predators (look for wounds or gaps in the house). The single most useful check is where the dead birds lie in the morning: piled in one corner, or scattered on their backs looking healthy.

Bean rust is a fungal disease showing as small reddish-brown to orange raised pustules, mostly on the undersides of leaves, that rub off as a rusty powder on the finger. Heavy infection yellows and drops leaves, cutting yield. It is favoured by humid, moderate-temperature weather and dense canopies. Manage by using resistant varieties, wider spacing and good airflow, rotating away from beans, and removing heavily infected debris. Fungicides exist for severe cases but must be applied at the label rate and timing with local guidance.

Cassava mosaic disease causes a yellow-and-green mottled or mosaic pattern on leaves, leaf distortion and curling, and stunted plants with reduced root yield. It is spread by whiteflies and, importantly, by planting cuttings taken from infected plants. The most effective control for smallholders is to plant clean, disease-free cuttings of tolerant or resistant varieties and to remove (rogue) diseased plants early. There is no spray that cures the virus.

Late blight of tomato appears as large, dark, water-soaked patches on leaves and stems that spread quickly in cool, wet, humid weather, often with a pale mould on the underside of lesions, and firm brown rot on fruit. It can destroy a crop within days. Remove and destroy affected plants, improve airflow and avoid overhead watering late in the day, and rotate away from tomato and potato. Protective fungicides help when applied before heavy infection, always at label rates.

Blossom end rot is a leathery dark sunken patch at the bottom (blossom end) of tomato fruit. It is not an infection but a calcium-supply problem driven by uneven watering — the plant cannot move enough calcium to the fruit when soil moisture swings between dry and wet. Correct by watering evenly and mulching to hold moisture, and avoid over-heavy nitrogen that pushes fast growth. Affected fruit will not recover but later fruit can be clean.

Stored maize is attacked by weevils and the larger grain borer, which bore into grain leaving fine flour and holes, and by moulds when grain is stored damp. Dry grain thoroughly before storage — it should be hard and not dent — and store in clean, sealed containers or hermetic bags that starve insects of air. Keep the store off the floor and away from old infested grain. For any storage pesticide follow the label exactly and keep it away from food and children; hermetic storage often avoids chemicals altogether.

Aflatoxins are toxins produced by Aspergillus moulds on maize and groundnuts that are poorly dried or stored damp, and they are a serious human and animal health risk that cannot be seen or tasted reliably. Reduce risk by harvesting on time, drying quickly to a safe moisture, sorting out damaged and mouldy grains, and storing dry and cool. Do not eat or feed visibly mouldy grain. There is no safe home treatment to remove aflatoxin once present.

A sudden, field-wide yellowing right after heavy rain usually points to the rain rather than a disease. Waterlogging saturates the soil and starves roots of air, and it leaches nitrogen below the root zone, so the whole crop pales at once rather than in spreading spots. A disease more typically starts in patches and spreads. Improve drainage, avoid compacting wet soil, and top-dress nitrogen once the soil drains and the crop is actively growing again.

Striga (witchweed) is a parasitic plant that attaches to cereal roots and drains the crop, causing stunting and yellowing even where soil looks adequately fertilised, with small bright-flowered weeds emerging near affected plants. It is worst on poor, low-nitrogen soils. Management combines improving soil fertility and organic matter, rotation or intercropping with legumes that reduce the Striga seed bank, hand-pulling before the weed sets seed, and Striga-tolerant varieties.

Basic biosecurity protects a smallholder flock from most disease disasters. Keep newly bought or returning birds separate for a couple of weeks before mixing them, limit visitors and shared equipment, provide clean water and clean feeders daily, control rodents and wild-bird access, and remove dead birds promptly and safely. When several birds die suddenly, treat it as a possible notifiable disease such as Newcastle, isolate the flock, and contact a veterinary or extension officer rather than moving birds.

AgriDoc never invents a pesticide or veterinary drug dose, rate, or price. Product strengths and safe rates vary by formulation, target and country, and a wrong dose is wasteful and dangerous to the user, the crop, the animals and the people who eat the produce. For any chemical or medicine, follow the rate printed on the product label for your specific product and confirm with a local agricultural extension officer or veterinarian, spray on calm dry days with protective clothing, and consider mechanical or cultural control first.

Foot-and-mouth disease is a highly contagious viral disease of cattle and other cloven-hoofed animals. Signs come on fast: heavy drooling, fever, going off feed, a sharp drop in milk, and blisters (vesicles) on the tongue, gums, muzzle and between the claws that break into raw sores, so animals are lame and reluctant to move; young calves may die. It spreads quickly by contact and movement, is notifiable, and has no cure. Isolate affected stock, do not move, sell or slaughter them, and report at once. Meanwhile most adults recover with simple support: offer soft feed and clean water and rest them on soft, dry ground, since the mouth and foot sores make eating and walking painful.

Contagious bovine pleuropneumonia is a serious bacterial (Mycoplasma) lung disease of cattle that is usually chronic. Look for a dry, painful cough and fast, laboured breathing that worsens with movement; fever, nasal discharge, and animals standing with the neck stretched out and elbows turned away from the chest, grunting as they breathe. Some recover but carry and spread the germ while looking near-normal. It passes by close contact and coughing, so it travels with animal movement and trading. It is notifiable: isolate affected and newly bought cattle, avoid moving stock, and report to a veterinary officer, who decides on treatment or vaccination. Meanwhile keep sick animals rested and drinking, and do not drive them.

Lumpy skin disease is a viral disease of cattle spread mainly by biting insects and ticks, so outbreaks follow wet, insect-heavy seasons. Affected animals run a fever, then develop firm, raised skin nodules over the body — head, neck, udder and legs — that may ulcerate and scab; the lymph nodes swell, the eyes and nose run, and milk drops. It is notifiable: isolate affected and newly bought cattle, avoid moving stock, and report to a veterinary officer. Most animals recover with support — keep the open nodules clean, control the flies feeding on the sores, and keep the animal eating and drinking. A vaccine is the main protection; its schedule and handling follow the label and veterinary advice.

Blackleg is a clostridial disease (Clostridium chauvoei) that strikes young, thriving, well-grown cattle at pasture, often the best animals. Soil spores are taken in and lodge in muscle; the first sign is usually sudden lameness with a hot, painful swelling on a hindquarter or shoulder that soon turns cold and crackles with gas when pressed. Fever, dullness and collapse follow, and most die within a day, sometimes just found dead. It is not passed animal-to-animal but comes from contaminated ground. A vaccine reliably prevents it — discuss its use with a vet. Because sudden pasture deaths can also be anthrax, do not open a suspect carcass; report it and dispose of it safely.

When a cow that seemed healthy is found suddenly dead, sometimes with dark, tarry blood that will not clot oozing from the nose, mouth or back passage, suspect anthrax. Do not open, cut or skin the carcass and do not eat or move it — the bacteria form hardy spores when exposed to air, and anthrax passes to people. Report the death at once to a veterinary or extension officer, who will confirm it and guide safe disposal, often by burning or deep burial. A vaccine exists for at-risk areas; its schedule and handling must follow the label and local veterinary advice.

Cows that abort in late pregnancy, or that hold the afterbirth and then discharge, may be carrying brucellosis, especially where several animals lose calves in one season. The germ spreads through birth fluids, the aborted calf and membranes, and raw milk, and it also sickens people with long, recurring fevers. Wear gloves and wash well when handling calvings, abortions and afterbirths, and bury or burn this material rather than letting dogs or other cows contact it. Always boil or pasteurise milk before drinking. There is no home cure; report repeated abortions to a veterinary or extension officer, who can test the herd and advise.

A dairy cow with one quarter of the udder hot, hard and swollen, giving milk with clots, flakes, watery strings or blood, has mastitis. Catch it early by drawing the first squirts from each teat onto a strip-cup or dark surface before milking — abnormal foremilk shows there first. Milk affected cows last, discard their milk, and wash and dry hands and udders between cows to stop spread. Keep bedding clean and dry, and dip or spray teats after milking. A cow may need antibiotics, but the choice, dose and withdrawal period must be set by a veterinarian — do not self-prescribe or sell milk during treatment.

East Coast fever is a tick-borne disease of cattle, carried by the brown ear tick, and it hits introduced and young stock hardest. A sick animal runs a high fever, and the lymph nodes — first in front of the ear, then at the shoulder and flank — swell into felt lumps; later come laboured breathing, a frothy nose and rapid loss of condition. Treatment exists but works best given early, so report cases fast to a veterinarian. While you arrange help, check the ears and body and remove any ticks by hand, and keep the animal shaded, watered and eating. Prevent it by controlling ticks with dipping or spraying and keeping new arrivals separate; a vaccination method exists in some areas.

In areas with tsetse flies, cattle that grow steadily thinner despite feeding well may have trypanosomiasis, also called nagana. The parasite, spread by the fly's bite, destroys red blood cells, so the gums, eye membranes and vulva look pale, the coat stares, and animals tire easily; some show on-and-off fever and swollen glands under the jaw. Look here first: an ox that is pale and thin though it keeps eating points to nagana rather than simple hunger. Drugs to treat it exist, but the choice and dose must come from a veterinarian, so report failing animals for testing early. Meanwhile keep them well fed and rested and cut fly contact by grazing away from thick tsetse bush.

Peste des petits ruminants (PPR, or 'goat plague') is a highly contagious viral disease of goats and sheep. Affected animals run a sudden high fever, then watery eye and nose discharge that crusts over, sores in the mouth, coughing and laboured breathing, and profuse, foul-smelling diarrhoea; deaths can be heavy in young stock. PPR is notifiable — isolate sick animals, keep new stock separate, and report suspected outbreaks rather than moving animals. Meanwhile give supportive care that saves some animals: offer oral rehydration fluid (clean water with a little salt and sugar) against the dehydration, and soft feed as the mouth sores make eating painful. A vaccine exists; its schedule follows the label and a vet.

Contagious caprine pleuropneumonia (CCPP) is a severe, highly contagious bacterial lung disease of goats caused by a Mycoplasma. Sick goats stand with the head and neck extended, breathe fast and with obvious effort, grunt or cough painfully, run a high fever and often stop eating; many die, some quickly after only a short illness. It spreads by close contact and coughing in crowded or newly mixed herds. Isolate affected goats, avoid moving stock, and call a veterinary or extension officer promptly, as CCPP is notifiable in many areas. Meanwhile keep sick goats rested, shaded and drinking and do not drive them, as effort worsens the breathing. Antibiotics and a vaccine exist, but the dose and withdrawal period must be set by a veterinarian.

Orf (contagious ecthyma) is a viral skin disease that causes thick, scabby, wart-like sores on the lips, muzzle and gums of lambs and kids, and sometimes on the teats of nursing dams. Sore-mouthed young may struggle to suckle and lose condition, but the disease is usually self-limiting and heals over a few weeks; keep affected animals feeding and watch for maggots or secondary infection in the scabs. Orf is zoonotic and can cause painful sores on people's hands, so wear gloves when handling affected animals and wash well afterwards. Isolate sore-mouthed young and do not mix them with clean stock until they have healed.

Sheep pox and goat pox are serious, highly contagious viral diseases showing fever, dullness and off-feed animals, then firm, raised pox lesions most visible on the hairless face, lips, eyelids, udder and inner legs, which scab and can scar. Breathing may be affected when lesions form in the airways, and young animals often die. It spreads by close contact and contaminated housing. Isolate sick animals, keep newly bought stock separate, and do not move animals off the farm — these are notifiable in many areas, so report suspected cases. Meanwhile keep sick animals feeding and drinking, keep the lesions clean, and control flies to give them the best chance.

Foot rot is a bacterial infection of the hoof that spreads in wet, muddy conditions and causes lameness, often in several animals at once. Affected feet smell foul and rotten, and the horn of the sole and heel becomes under-run and separates from the tissue below, frequently starting in the skin between the claws. Move animals to dry, clean footing and carefully trim away loose, under-run horn to open the infection to the air. A foot bath helps, but the solution and its strength should follow the product label and local veterinary advice; do not guess a concentration. Isolate and treat lame animals, and avoid bringing foot rot home on newly bought stock.

Haemonchosis, caused by the barber's pole worm (Haemonchus contortus), is a blood-sucking stomach worm of sheep and goats that drains the animal without usually causing diarrhoea. Because it feeds on blood, the signs are those of anaemia: pale gums and inner eyelids, weakness, poor growth, and sometimes a soft fluid swelling under the jaw called bottle jaw. It is worst in the warm, wet season when pasture larvae surge. Check eyelid colour regularly using the FAMACHA card as a field anaemia test, and treat only the pale, affected animals. A dewormer is effective, but the product, dose and withdrawal period must follow the label and a local veterinarian's advice.

Coccidiosis is caused by Eimeria parasites that damage the gut lining of young, crowded kids, lambs and calves, usually around weaning or after a move. The main sign is diarrhoea, sometimes dark or bloody, with straining, poor growth and a rough coat; badly affected young stock can dehydrate and die. Older animals often carry it without signs but seed the pens. Act early: offer oral rehydration fluid (clean water with a little salt and sugar) to fight the dehydration, keep bedding dry, avoid overcrowding, clean troughs off the ground, and separate scouring animals. Effective treatments exist, but the product, dose and course must follow the label and a vet's advice — never guess.

Dewormers (anthelmintics) still work, but worms are becoming resistant where the same product is used too often on every animal. Do not drench the whole flock blindly on a fixed calendar. Instead, treat the animals that need it — the young, the thin, and those the FAMACHA eyelid check flags as anaemic — so some worms in untreated animals stay susceptible and dilute resistance. Rotate between different drug classes only on a vet's advice, and dose to the heaviest animal in the group at the label rate rather than guessing and under-dosing. Combine treatment with pasture rotation and good nutrition; do not rely on the drench alone.

source: FAO — Tick and tick-borne disease control
text: Ticks weaken animals by feeding on blood and, more importantly, spread serious diseases such as East Coast fever, anaplasmosis, babesiosis and heartwater, so tick control is really disease prevention. Inspect animals often, especially the ears, tail, udder, brisket and between the legs where ticks gather, and remove them by hand, pulling straight out so the mouthparts do not break off. Where tick pressure is high, dips, sprays or pour-on acaricides help, but the product, strength and interval must follow the label and local veterinary advice to avoid resistance and residues. Rotate or rest pastures and clear brush to lower the tick burden.

Mange is caused by tiny mites (sarcoptic or psoroptic) that burrow in or feed on the skin. The hallmark is intense itching: animals rub, scratch and bite at themselves, losing hair in patches and developing thickened, crusty, wrinkled skin, often first on the head, ears, neck and legs. It spreads by direct contact and through shared housing, rubbing posts and equipment, so it can run through a herd quickly. Isolate affected animals early, and treat under veterinary direction — effective acaricides and injectables exist, but the product, dose and repeat interval must follow the label and a vet's advice. Clean and rest contaminated pens.

Pigs of any age going off feed with high fever, huddling together, and reddened or blotchy purple skin on the ears, belly and legs — then sudden death sweeping through the herd within days — point to African swine fever. It spreads by contact with sick pigs, contaminated feed or swill, and soft ticks; there is no cure and no field vaccine. Do not treat, sell or move sick pigs. Isolate the herd, keep visitors and new pigs out, cook or avoid swill, and report the deaths at once to a veterinary or extension officer. Clean and disinfect pens, clothing and vehicles between visits.

Classical swine fever (hog cholera) looks much like African swine fever in the field: fever, huddling, loss of appetite, weakness and staggering, sometimes diarrhoea and reddened skin, with high mortality in unvaccinated herds. The two cannot be told apart by eye — only a laboratory can confirm which one it is, so both must be reported. A vaccine exists in some areas and can protect healthy pigs, but the choice, schedule and handling must follow the vaccine label and a local veterinarian or extension officer. Isolate affected pigs, stop all movement and sales, and do not rely on antibiotics, which do not cure this virus.

Pigs that eat well but grow slowly, with a rough staring coat, pot belly and pale gums, are often carrying worms; large pale roundworms are sometimes seen in the dung, and heavy burdens in piglets can cause coughing or gut upset. Worm eggs build up on damp, dirty floors and are picked up from contaminated ground and feed. Keep floors clean, dry and well drained, remove dung daily, feed off the ground, and give clean water. Effective dewormers exist, but the product, dose and timing should follow the label and a veterinarian's or extension officer's advice; rotate pens and rest ground where possible.

source: FAO — pig housing and heat management
text: Pigs cannot sweat, so in hot weather they overheat quickly — panting, lying flat, crowding shade and going off feed, with sows at risk of heat stress and poor breeding. Give constant access to clean drinking water and shade, and a wallow or a wetted, well-drained area so pigs can cool themselves. Build housing with good airflow, a roof that keeps out sun and rain, and a floor that stays clean and dry, sloped so urine and washing water drain away. Do not overcrowd, provide separate space to isolate sick or newly bought pigs, and clean pens regularly.

In the first hours of life piglets must suckle colostrum — the first thick milk — which gives them energy and the antibodies that protect them until their own immunity develops; a piglet that misses it often fades and dies. Keep the farrowing area warm, dry and draught-free, since newborn piglets chill easily, and make sure weak piglets reach a teat. Piglets raised indoors on floors without soil can become anaemic and need supplemental iron, but the product, form and dose must be set by a veterinarian or extension officer. Handle piglets gently, keep bedding clean, and watch for scouring.

A newborn calf, kid or lamb is born with almost no immunity and depends entirely on colostrum — the thick first milk from its own mother — to survive its early weeks. Make sure the newborn suckles, or is helped to suckle, within the first few hours of birth, because the gut absorbs these protective antibodies best while very fresh and this window closes quickly. A weak newborn that cannot stand should be helped to the teat or fed the dam's milked colostrum. Keep it warm, dry and out of wind and rain, and dip or spray the navel to stop infection entering the cord.

Scours (watery diarrhoea) in a young calf, kid or lamb is common, and the real danger is not the diarrhoea itself but the dehydration it causes — a scouring newborn can weaken and die quickly if fluids are not replaced. The animal looks dull, its eyes sink, the skin is slow to spring back, and it stops sucking. Act early: give oral rehydration fluid (clean water with added salts and sugar) little and often, keep the newborn warm and dry, and keep it drinking. Do not withhold the dam's milk. Seek a veterinarian if the dung is bloody, the animal is very weak, cannot stand, or is not improving.

source: FAO — Livestock body condition and feeding
text: You cannot judge an animal's condition by eye alone under a thick coat — you have to feel it. Run your hand over the ribs, backbone and hip bones: sharp, easily felt bones mean the animal is too thin, while bones you cannot feel under a thick fat cover mean it is too fat. Aim for a middle score where bones are felt with light pressure. Provide enough good forage, clean water at all times, and free access to salt or a mineral lick. Change feeds gradually over several days, never suddenly, because an abrupt switch to rich or lush feed can trigger dangerous bloat. Score animals regularly so you catch a slide early.

Most herd and flock diseases arrive with a new animal or come home on one that has been to a market or another farm. Keep any newly bought or returning animal separate from the rest for a few weeks and watch it for coughing, scouring, sores or weight loss before letting it mix. Do not share needles between animals, and clean shared equipment such as ropes and feed troughs between uses. Provide clean water and dry, uncrowded housing, and keep feed off the ground away from droppings. If an animal dies suddenly or several die at once, do not move or sell stock — isolate the others and report it to a veterinary or extension officer.

Some animal diseases pass to people, so take simple precautions. Boil or pasteurise milk from animals whose health status you do not know before drinking it or giving it to children. Wash your hands after handling stock, and wear gloves when helping at a birth, touching sores or wounds, or handling a sick animal. Never eat an animal that died of an unknown illness, and dispose of carcasses by deep burial or as your officer advises so dogs and scavengers cannot reach them. If a suddenly dead animal is a possible anthrax case, do not open or cut the carcass — the blood and spores are dangerous to you — and call a veterinary or extension officer.

Rice blast, caused by the fungus Magnaporthe oryzae, shows on leaves as spindle- or diamond-shaped lesions with grey-to-whitish centres and brown margins that enlarge and merge in wet, humid weather. The dangerous form is neck rot: the neck just below the panicle turns brown-black, so the panicle whitens, stands upright and fills with empty grain. To tell neck blast from stem-borer whitehead, pull the head; a borer leaves a hollow, frass-filled tunnel, while blast shows a rotted brown neck with no tunnel. Manage with resistant varieties, balanced nitrogen without excess, good drainage and clearing infected stubble; for any fungicide follow the label rate and local extension guidance.

Rice yellow mottle virus causes yellow-green mottling and streaking of leaves, stunting, reduced tillering and poorly filled panicles, and badly hit plants may fail to head. It is spread mainly by chewing beetles, and by sap moving on hands, tools and irrigation water, so damage often starts at field edges and spreads in patches. Tell it from nitrogen deficiency, which is uniform and begins on older leaves: this mottling is uneven, comes with stunting and leaf twisting, and worsens where beetles feed. No spray cures the virus. Use tolerant varieties, rogue infected plants and weedy grass hosts early, control beetles on extension advice, and avoid carrying sap between fields.

Red-billed quelea are weaver birds that move in huge flocks and strip ripening heads of sorghum, pearl millet, rice and wheat, threshing out the soft milky grain and leaving empty glumes. To tell bird damage from smut, look at the head: quelea leave clean stripped or shattered grain, while smut leaves blackened galls of spore powder. Because flocks roost and breed communally, control works best when neighbours act together: scare birds from milk stage to harvest with noise, moving people and reflectors, grow early, uniform-maturing varieties so grain does not stand ripe alone, and avoid small isolated plots near reedbeds and roosts. Large-scale lethal control at colonies is organised by national authorities, not individual farmers.

Maize lethal necrosis arises when maize chlorotic mottle virus infects together with a cereal potyvirus such as sugarcane mosaic virus; the two reinforce each other, so damage is far worse than either alone. Look for chlorotic mottling spreading from the leaf base, dying leaf margins, a rotted dead heart in the whorl, severe stunting, and small, malformed or barren cobs, with early-infected plants often dying. It spreads through insect vectors, contaminated seed and crop residue. There is no cure, and it is a notifiable emerging disease, so report cases to extension or plant-health authorities. Prevent it with clean certified seed, tolerant varieties, a maize-free break in rotation, removing volunteers, and vector control on extension advice.

Grey leaf spot, caused by Cercospora fungi (C. zeae-maydis and, in Africa, often C. zeina), makes narrow, rectangular grey-to-tan lesions that run between the leaf veins and stop sharply at them, giving a blocky, ruler-edged look. It thrives in warm, humid areas where maize residue is left on the surface under continuous maize. To tell it from northern leaf blight, note that blight lesions are large cigar-shaped ellipses crossing the veins, while grey leaf spot stays boxed between them. Heavy infection dries leaves and weakens stalks. Manage with resistant varieties, rotation away from maize, and removing old maize trash that carries the fungus over; for any fungicide follow the label rate and local extension guidance.

source: Wikipedia — Cassava brown streak virus disease
text: Cassava brown streak disease first shows as a yellow blotchy mottle along the leaf veins, often on older leaves, but the damage that ruins the crop is inside: cut a storage root and you find dry, brown, corky necrosis streaking through the flesh, sometimes with pitting on the skin. This distinguishes it from cassava mosaic, which mottles leaves but usually leaves roots usable. The virus spreads through whiteflies and, above all, by planting cuttings from infected plants. There is no cure spray. Plant clean, certified cuttings of tolerant varieties, rogue and destroy affected plants early, and control whiteflies as your extension officer advises.

Cassava bacterial blight begins as angular, water-soaked spots on the leaves that are boxed in by the veins, later browning and merging with yellow margins; leaves wilt and drop, shoots die back from the tip, and drops of gum may ooze from stems and leaf stalks. The angular, vein-limited spots and the gum help tell it from fungal leaf spots, which look more rounded. It moves in infected cuttings, on tools, and by rain splash, worsening in wet weather. Plant clean cuttings of tolerant varieties from healthy fields, rogue diseased plants, rotate, avoid working the crop when wet, and disinfect cutting tools.

Banana Xanthomonas wilt (BXW), which also strikes enset, shows as yellowing and wilting of leaves, uneven and premature fruit ripening with rusty internal staining, and a tell-tale yellow bacterial ooze that beads from the cut surface when you slit an infected pseudostem. It spreads on contaminated cutting tools, by insects visiting the male bud, and in infected suckers. Remove the male bud (debud) with a forked stick rather than a knife, disinfect or flame cutting tools between every plant and mat, cut out and destroy whole infected mats in place, use clean planting material, and stop moving suckers from affected gardens.

Black Sigatoka is a fungal leaf disease of banana and plantain that thrives in warm, wet, humid conditions. It starts as thin reddish-brown to black streaks running along the leaf, which widen into dark blotches with yellow halos, merge, and kill the leaf; badly affected plants lose their canopy, yield less, and ripen fruit prematurely and unevenly. Cut off and destroy the most affected leaves, improve air movement and drainage by weeding and avoiding overcrowded stands, and grow tolerant cultivars where available. If a fungicide is considered, follow the product label rate and local extension guidance, and never guess a dose.

The sweet potato weevil is a small, slender, ant-like beetle with a long snout; its larvae tunnel through vines and storage roots, and the roots react with bitter compounds that make even lightly attacked tubers foul-tasting and unsellable. Damage is worst in dry, cracked soils where weevils reach the roots, and infestation carries over in tubers left in the ground and in cuttings. Plant clean, weevil-free vine-tip cuttings, rotate away from last season's plots, hill up soil to close cracks over developing roots, harvest promptly instead of leaving roots in the ground, destroy volunteers, residues and culls, and store only sound, uninfested roots.

Cowpea aphids are small, shiny black, soft-bodied insects that cluster on growing shoots, flower stalks and young pods, sucking sap so tips wilt, curl and stunt. Their sticky honeydew coats the leaves and a black sooty mould grows on it, and the same aphids carry viruses from plant to plant. Scout young plants often, especially in dry spells. Spare the ladybird beetles, hoverfly larvae and tiny parasitic wasps that eat aphids, grow tolerant or resistant varieties, and pinch out badly infested tips early. For any insecticide, follow the product label rate and local extension guidance; never guess a dose.

The legume pod borer (Maruca) attacks cowpea at flowering: caterpillars web together buds, flowers and young pods with silk and frass, then bore inside, so a pod that looks sound can hide a caterpillar and hollowed seeds. Open a few webbed flowers and pods to confirm the grub within. Scout from the first flower buds, since damage is heaviest during flowering and early pod set, and pick out webbed clusters by hand. Grow earlier, uniform crops to shorten the flowering window, keep fields weeded, and spare natural enemies. For any insecticide, follow the product label rate and local extension guidance; never guess a dose.

Cowpea and bean seed holed in storage is usually the work of bruchid beetles (cowpea weevil, Callosobruchus): adults lay eggs on the seed, grubs tunnel inside, and neat round exit holes with fine dust appear as they emerge, ruining a seed lot within weeks. Dry the grain hard before storing, then keep it in airtight, hermetic containers or bags that starve the insects of air; solar heating the seed in a clear sealed bag under strong sun kills eggs and grubs already inside. Store well away from old infested stock. For any storage pesticide follow the label exactly and keep it away from food and children.

Bean anthracnose shows as dark brown to black sunken spots on pods, often with a slightly raised darker rim and a pinkish ooze in wet weather, plus brick-red to black lesions along the veins on the leaf undersides and dark streaks on stems. It is carried on and in the seed and spreads in cool, wet, splashing conditions, so outbreaks often trace back to a saved, infected seed lot. Plant certified or clean seed saved from a healthy crop, rotate away from beans for a season or more, avoid working among plants while wet, and remove infected debris. Use resistant varieties where available.

Groundnut rosette disease stunts plants and turns leaves yellow or mottled, with small, bunched, distorted leaflets that give a bushy rosette look; plants hit early stay dwarfed and yield little. It is a virus complex spread by aphids (the same black cowpea aphid), not by seed, so it builds up where aphids thrive on late or thinly planted crops. No spray cures the virus. Plant early and at a good, even stand so the canopy closes fast and fewer aphids settle, use tolerant or resistant varieties, rogue out diseased plants, and keep the crop weeded and vigorous.

Tomato plants that wilt suddenly while the leaves stay green, often one side or the whole plant collapsing in hot weather, point to bacterial wilt. Confirm it with a simple field test: cut a piece of the lower stem, look for a brown ring in the water-conducting tissue, and hang the cut end in a glass of clear water — cloudy, milky threads streaming from the cut mean bacteria. There is no cure. Pull and destroy affected plants, avoid moving soil or water from the spot, rotate away from tomato and other solanaceous crops, and where the disease is common plant resistant varieties or graft onto resistant rootstock.

Pale, winding or blotchy mines inside tomato leaves that later turn into brown papery patches, together with small holes and tunnels bored into stems and fruit, are typical of the tomato leafminer (Tuta absoluta), a moth whose larvae feed inside the plant. Because they live protected inside leaves and fruit, prevention and early action matter most. Hang pheromone traps to detect and monitor the moths, pick off and destroy mined leaves and infested fruit, remove crop residues after harvest, and rotate with non-solanaceous crops. If an insecticide is needed, choose and apply it strictly to the product label and local extension advice; never guess a dose, and rotate chemical groups to slow resistance.

Small pale-green caterpillars that wriggle and drop on silken threads when the leaf is touched, leaving windowpane patches where they scrape the underside and small shot holes, are diamondback moth larvae on cabbage, kale and other brassicas. Scout the growing points and leaf undersides regularly and act while numbers are low. Protect natural enemies such as parasitic wasps by avoiding routine broad-spectrum sprays, which often make outbreaks worse. Remove old brassica stalks and volunteer plants after harvest, rotate away from brassicas, and consider intercropping. If control is needed, favour selective or biological products chosen with local extension, applied to the label; never guess a dose, and rotate products to delay resistance.

Small brown spots on cocoa pods that quickly spread into a hard, blackish rot covering the pod, often with a whitish bloom of spores in wet weather, are black pod disease, caused by Phytophthora, a fungus-like water mould. It thrives in the rainy season and spreads by rain splash and contact. Harvest ripe pods frequently and completely, and cut out and bury or remove diseased and mummified pods so they do not seed new infections. Prune trees and shade to open the canopy and let pods dry faster, and improve drainage. Copper-based fungicides can help in bad seasons but must follow the product label and local extension guidance; never guess a dose.

Yellow-orange powdery patches on the undersides of coffee leaves, matching pale yellow blotches on top, that later dry brown and cause leaves to drop early, are coffee leaf rust caused by the fungus Hemileia vastatrix. Heavy defoliation weakens trees and cuts the next harvest. Where rust is a regular problem, plant resistant varieties, and open the canopy and shade by pruning so leaves dry faster and air moves through. Keep trees vigorous with good nutrition and weeding, and remove heavily infected leaf litter. Copper or other fungicides help in severe years but only when applied at the label rate and timing with local extension advice; never guess a dose.

source: FAO — Soil fertility and organic matter
text: Tired soil shows itself in the crop: pale, slow, uneven growth, a thin dark topsoil, hard crusting that sheds water instead of soaking it up, and yields that fall season after season even in good rains. Rebuild organic matter first, because it holds moisture and feeds the living soil. Return crop residues to the field, add well-rotted compost or animal manure, and grow legumes such as beans, cowpea or groundnut that fix nitrogen from the air and can be dug in as green manure. Keep the ground covered to slow erosion. If you add mineral fertiliser, follow the product label rate and local extension guidance; never guess a dose.

Growing the same crop on the same land every season lets its pests, diseases and weeds build up in the soil until yields collapse. Break the cycle by rotating: follow a cereal like maize or sorghum with a legume such as beans, cowpea or groundnut, which also leaves nitrogen behind for the next crop. Intercropping mixes crops in one field so pests find their host plant less easily and ground cover shades out weeds. The push-pull idea plants a repellent legume like Desmodium between cereal rows and a trap grass around the edge to drive away stemborers and suppress Striga. Plan rotations over several seasons, not just one.

source: FAO — Seed quality and variety selection
text: The seed you plant sets the ceiling on your harvest, so start clean. Use certified seed where you can, or select your own only from healthy, high-yielding plants, keeping the plumpest grain and discarding anything shrivelled, discoloured or mouldy. Saving seed from diseased plants carries the trouble into next season, because many diseases, including bacterial blights and some viruses, travel on or inside the seed. Choose varieties suited to your rainfall and season length and, where available, ones bred to resist the pests and diseases common in your area. Store dry seed in sealed containers, safe from moisture and weevils, until planting.

Integrated pest management means acting on what you see, not spraying by the calendar. Walk your field regularly and scout, looking under leaves and into whorls, and identify the pest before you act, since natural enemies and harmless insects are easily mistaken for the culprit. Judge by how much damage is really present, because a few insects rarely need treatment. Lead with cultural and biological measures: resistant varieties, sanitation, rotation, hand-picking, and protecting the predators and parasites that control pests for free. Keep chemicals as the last resort, and when one is truly needed follow the product label rate and local extension guidance; never guess a dose.

Weeds hurt most while the crop is young, competing for light, water and nutrients during the first few weeks, so timely early weeding protects yield far more than late clearing does. Weed before the crop's critical early period closes over, keep field edges clean, and lay a mulch of crop residues to smother new weeds and hold soil moisture. Watch for Striga, a parasitic weed that attaches to the roots of maize, sorghum and millet and is worst on poor, nitrogen-depleted soils; hand-pull it before it flowers and sets seed, and build fertility and rotate with legumes to starve it out. If herbicides are used, follow the product label and local extension guidance.

Root-knot nematodes are tiny soil roundworms that swell plant roots into knots and galls, choking the flow of water and nutrients. Above ground you see patchy stunting, yellowing, midday wilting that recovers by night, and weak yield in scattered spots that spread each season. Lift a struggling plant and look for the tell-tale beaded galls to confirm, remembering these differ from the healthy round nitrogen nodules on legume roots. There is no cure once roots are galled. Rotate away from susceptible crops like tomato and many vegetables, use resistant varieties and clean, gall-free seedlings, add organic matter to feed natural enemies, and fallow or flood badly infested land.

A single early shower can be a false start: it wets only the surface, tempts you to plant, then dries out so the young seedlings die before the rains return. Judge the true onset not by the first storm but by whether the rains settle into a steady pattern that keeps the soil moist below the surface between showers. Lean on your area's usual seasonal calendar and the memory of older local farmers, and check with your nearest agro-met or extension officer. When in doubt, wait for the rains to establish before committing your main seed, and keep some seed back in case you must replant.

An uncertain season — one that may start late, break in the middle, or end early — is risky to bet on with a single planting. Spread the risk by staggering: sow part of your land when the rains first look settled and the rest a little later, rather than committing everything at once. Mixing separate plots, planting dates, and varieties of different maturity lengths means a dry spell or a false start hits only part of your crop, not all of it. Let your own reading of the rains and local extension advice guide each planting, rather than a fixed calendar date.

When the rains pause mid-season and the crop wilts in the heat of the day, the priority is holding on to the moisture already in the soil. Mulch the surface with crop residues, grass, or leaves to slow evaporation and keep roots cooler. Weed thoroughly, because weeds compete hard for what little water there is. Avoid disturbing the soil more than needed, and if you have a small water source, spot-water around the base of priority plants rather than wetting the whole field. These steps buy time until the rains return; watch your soil and take local agro-met and extension advice.

For a short or unreliable rainy season, the variety you choose spreads risk before you even plant. Early-maturing varieties race to fill grain and can finish before the rains stop, escaping a late-season dry spell, while drought-tolerant types hold up better through a mid-season break. Ask your local extension officer or seed supplier which varieties are bred for your area and season length, and keep some of the hardy local types that farmers here have relied on for generations. Where the season is very uncertain, plant a mix of maturity lengths so not all your crop depends on the rains lasting.

Much of the rain that falls runs off bare, sloping ground before it can soak in. Hold more of it by slowing runoff: dig simple contour bunds, planting basins, or trenches across the slope so water pools and sinks rather than racing away. Keep the soil covered with mulch or cover crops to cut evaporation and let rain infiltrate instead of crusting the surface. Where you can, channel roof runoff into a lined pit or tank for later use. Building up soil organic matter also helps the ground hold moisture. Match the method to your slope and soil with local extension guidance.

In the hot, dusty harmattan and dry season, plan for scarce water and drying winds: prioritise irrigation for high-value plots, mulch and shade seedbeds and nurseries, and time transplanting and heavy field work for the cooler parts of the day. Water livestock well and give them shade, as heat cuts feeding and growth. Stored grain and produce face the opposite risk when humidity rises at the turn of the season, as reabsorbed moisture brings moulds and weevils. Keep stores dry, ventilated and off the ground, dry grain fully before sealing it in clean airtight containers, and check often for damp or heating.

source: FAO — When to sell or store
text: Prices for most staple crops are usually at their lowest right after harvest, when everyone is selling at once, and often rise in the weeks and months that follow. If you can hold some grain, weigh the likely gain against storage costs and the risk of loss to pests, mould or theft, and against how urgently you need cash. Sell what you must now to meet real needs, and store the rest well if you can afford to wait. Check prices at several local buyers and markets yourself before deciding, and do not trust a single buyer's word.

Buyers pay more for clean, uniform produce, so a little sorting before sale often earns back the effort. Remove stones, soil, chaff, leaves and any rotten, broken, discoloured or insect-damaged pieces, and separate produce by size and quality into grades rather than selling everything mixed. Clean, dry, well-sorted grain also stores better and loses fewer sales to rejection. Present it in clean bags. Ask several buyers what quality they want and how they grade, so you can match your best produce to the buyer who values it, and never accept one buyer's claim that your crop is poor.

source: FAO — Grain drying and safe storage
text: Drying grain properly before storage is what lets you hold it and sell later without losing quality. Grain stored too moist grows mould and can develop aflatoxin, a hidden poison that spoils the crop and can get it rejected from better markets. Dry on clean mats or tarpaulins, not bare ground, until the grain is hard, then store in clean, dry, sealed containers or hermetic bags that keep out air, moisture and insects. Check stored grain regularly for heating, damp or pests. Well-dried, well-stored produce keeps its value and gives you the choice of when to sell.

A distress sale is when you are forced to sell in a hurry at whatever price is offered, usually because you need cash and cannot wait. Traders know this and may push a low price on farmers who seem desperate. Plan ahead so you are not cornered: keep a little cash or savings aside, spread sales over time rather than dumping everything at harvest, and learn roughly what buyers are paying before you talk. If a buyer pressures you to decide on the spot, that is a reason to pause, not to hurry. Check other buyers first.

source: FAO — Collective marketing and farmer groups
text: One farmer with a few bags has little bargaining power; many farmers pooling their harvest have much more. Selling together as a group or cooperative lets you offer the larger, steady volumes that bigger buyers want, share the cost of transport and storage, and negotiate from strength instead of taking the first offer. A group can also gather price information from several markets, so no member is sold a low price alone. Agree clear rules on grading, weighing, payment and shared costs in advance, and keep honest records, so members trust the arrangement and stay together.

You cannot tell profit from loss unless you know what the crop cost you. Keep a simple notebook of what you spend, including seed, fertiliser, labour, transport, storage, bags and any hired services, and what you earn from each sale. Over a season this shows which crops and which buyers actually pay, and warns you when a low offer would sell your work at a loss. It also helps you plan how much to sell now and how much to store. You do not need fancy accounts; steady, honest records of costs and sales are enough to decide better.

The surest way to have more and better produce to sell is to lose less of what you already grew. Crops are lost at every step, through shattering if harvested too late, spillage in handling, and spoilage from pests, damp and mould in storage. Harvest at the right maturity, handle gently to avoid bruising and cracking, dry properly, and store in clean, sealed, pest-proof containers off the ground. Every bag saved from rot or pests is a bag you can sell, and cleaner, sounder produce earns a better price. Cutting loss costs little and adds directly to what you sell.

When flooding or days of heavy rain leave water standing on the land, the first job is to get it off: open or clear drainage channels so air can reach the roots again, because plants left in waterlogged soil soon suffocate and rot at the base. Do not walk on or work very wet soil, as this compacts it and makes drainage even worse. On ground that floods most years, plant on ridges, mounds or raised beds so roots sit above the saturated layer, and shape the land to shed water before the wet season. Once the water has drained and fresh growth appears, judge whether thin or dying patches are worth replanting.
